abstract:
Glioblastoma is the most common primary brain cancer in adults, with a poor prognosis and median survival of 15 months after treatment. Few in vivo transgenic models exist for testing new therapeutics.
A novel mouse model for the classical subtype of human glioblastoma (GBM) has been bred using Cre-mediated EGFRvIII overexpression and homozygous p19-ARF deletion, the mouse homolog of human p14ARF/CDKN2A, in GFAP-expressing cells.
Transgenic mice developed intraparenchymal and/or leptomeningeal brain lesions as early as 1 month old and 95% of mice succumb to endpoint symptoms of hydrocephalus and/or paralysis by 6 months. Immunohistochemical analysis confirms EGFRvIII overexpression and p19-ARF loss in Cre-expressing cells, along with patchy positive GFAP and high proliferation by Ki67 as well as loss of H3K27me3. Bulk and single cell RNA sequencing revealed tumors cluster closely with classical GBM and have significant upregulation of downstream markers in the JAK/STAT and P13K/AKT pathways as well as intratumoral heterogeneity. Dissociated tumors generated xenograft tumors by 3 weeks post intracranial injections into NOD-SCID mice and were characteristic of the primary lesion.
We developed a spontaneous, immune-competent murine glioma model that enables characterization of tumor development within an intact immune microenvironment and provides a resource for future mechanistic studies.

Language="eng"><AbstractText>Glioblastoma is the most common primary brain cancer in adults, and few animal models accurately reproduce how this aggressive tumor develops in people. The authors of this study wanted to create a new mouse model that closely mirrors the classical form of human glioblastoma so it can be used to test new treatments. To do this, they genetically engineered mice so certain brain cells produced high levels of a cancer-driving protein and lost a key tumor-suppressing gene, then analyzed how tumors formed and compared their biological features to human tumors. They found that most mice developed brain tumors within months, the tumors shared important molecular characteristics with classical human glioblastoma, and tumor cells from these mice were able to grow new tumors when implanted into other mice.</AbstractText><CopyrightInformation>© The Author(s) 2026.
